3. It is noted that the Defendant No.1 entered appearance in the Suit and incidentally both the parties on 21.9.2008 filed a petition for Compromise of the Suit and consequently both parties deposed before the learned Court in support of the said compromise. The plaintiff-petitioner states that prior to filing the Compromise Petition, the Defendant No. 1 filed a Written Statement denying material allegations made in the plaint contending that there is no cause of action and that the Suit is not maintainable and disavowing the plaintiff-petitioner's statement that he is the owner and in possession of the Suit land. 

 5. It is evident to this Court from documents on record and, in particular, Annexure-E to this Application, that consequent upon the Compromise petition of 21.9.2008 the Defendant No. 1, however, filed a petition dated 23.9.2008 seeking a postponement of issuance of any Order on the Compromise petition on account of an alleged breach of trust by her husband the plaintiff-petitioner in duly complying with his undertaking in her favour evidenced in the Compromise petition. It is on the heels of these developments that the Defendant No. 1 passed away on 10.10.2008. It is against this backdrop that the Opposite party being Md. Moklisur Rahman, given the apparent transfer pendente lite of the Suit land to hint on 26.12.2007 and 20.4.2008, filed an Application under Order 1, Rule 10 of the Code seeking to be added as a party and further reinforcing that prayer by bringing forth the fact of being a necessary and proper party stemming from title and interest in the Suit land on account of the transfer pendente lite. 

 8. The learned Advocate for the Opposite party No. 1 Mr. Chanchal Kumar Biswas, in responding to the Rule, highlights that the issue of title to the Suit land was a highly contested one between the plaintiff-petitioner and the now deceased Defendant No. l. This, Mr. Biswas explain, is evident, for example, from the Written Statement filed on 10.8.2008 that in disputing the plaintiff-petitioner's claim to the Suit land instead asserts the ownership and possession of the same to lie with the Defendant No. 1 by her own right and in her own name. Submitting on the fact of the compromise struck as above stated by and between the plaintiff-petitioner and the Defendant No. 1, Mr. Biswas lays stress, however, on the developments of 23.9.2008 reflected in an Order of that date whereby the Defendant No. 1 sought to put a halt to effect being given to the Compromise Petition of 21.9.2008 on account of breach of its terms already committed by the plaintiff-petitioner. Mr. Biswas submits as dubious the effort thereafter of the plaintiff-petitioner to, however, contrive to convince the Court that the Defendant No. 1 was in that regard not pressing her above referred petition of 23.9.2008. In doing so, the plaintiff-apparently prayed concomitantly for the suit to be decreed on the terms of the very Compromise petition that the Defendant No. 1 had earlier so raised an objection to. 

 Indeed, as argued by Mr. Md. Zakir Hossain, the core principle still remains of a sale pendente lite resulting in sub ordinate rights relative to the rights decreed upon ultimately in the suit proceeding s. In broadening, however, the scope of the application of the Doctrine in a beneficial sense it has equally been judicially endorsed that the effect of section 52 of the Act, however, is not to completely wipe out a sale pendente lite. It is from that notion that there emerges the concept, in certain circumstances at least, of the adequate protection of interests and rights pendent elite keeping nevertheless within the broader framework of the principle of subordination as above stated. Accordingly, the Supreme Court of India in Nagubai Ammal and others vs. B Shama Rao and others reported in AIR 1956 (SC) 593 ruled in simple terms thus: 

 "The effect of section 52 is not to wipe out a sale pendent elite altogether but to subordinate it to the rights based on the decree in the suit." 

 11. Predicated on that reading of the core concept of the Doctrine of Lis Pendens the supreme Court, thereafter, referred to view the operation of section 52 of the Act in terms that a transfer pendente lite is indeed "good except to the extent that it might conflict with rights decreed under the relevant decree or order." The Indian supreme Court's decision further Sm Saila Bala Dassi vs. Sm Nirmala Sundari Dassi and another reported in AIR 1958 (SC) 394 takes the beneficial application of the Doctrine a notch further in that since the transferee pendente lite shall in any event be bound by proceedings initiated by the parties in whose favour a decree is passed in execution of the decree it would indeed be in the interest of justice that such transferee pendente use by given on opportunity to protect his/her rights. 

 13. Turning to the provisions of Order 1, Rule 10(2) of the Code, this Court appreciates that first and foremost it reflects a judicial discretion that has to be exercised with regard to impleading a party or not in view of the fact and circumstances of each individual case. It is equally to he borne in mind that any applicant under order 1, Rule 10(2) may either qualify as a necessary and/or a proper party. Hence, should the facts and circumstances merit identifying an applicant as one or the other kind of party then that would merit a favourable exercise of judicial discretion. Here, this Court is reminded of the fact that a necessary party is one whose presence in a suit is otherwise enjoined by law or in whose absence no effective decree can be passed. Contradistinctively, a proper party is one whose presence though not necessary for passing an effective decree, may nevertheless remain central in order to facilitate a more effectual and complete adjudication of all the disputes and thereby necessarily help avoid a multiplicity' of Proceedings (See Mahmudul Islam and probir Neogi "The Law of Civil procedure" Volume-1, page, 519). Upon a perusal of the impugned order of the learned Joint District Judge it is evident that it is the latter rationale of impleading a proper party that appears to have been the guiding force in his arriving at the decision that he did. It is here that Mr. Biswas has satisfactorily established certain compelling circumstances in this Case under which the Opposite Party No. 1 would indeed qualify to be added on as a proper party. It is noted that the Opposite party No.1, since the demise of the Defendant No. 1 on 10.10.2008, has been virtually the only interested party in place of the deceased Defendant No. 1 to agitate and deliberate upon the competing rights and interests in the Suit land. This is so given that the Defendant No. 1 passed away without leaving any children but instead certain of her siblings who in the facts, have not acquired as direct a right and interest in the Suit property as the Opposite Party No. 1 has. Accordingly, the Opposite party No I now reasonably apprehends that without being impleaded as a party a decree may ensile that, will not ensure justice overall. These facts manifest in effect some of the tests that can be discerned from the various judgments cited by Mr. Biswas, these being chiefly the judgments in the mokthar Masum Abedin Case and in Anil Ranjan Ghosh vs. Assistant Custodian reported in 49 DLR (1997), 296. It is noted that in the Anil Ranjan Ghosh Case the notion subscribed to was that of the necessity of impleading a party (like the Opposite party No. 1 in this instant Case) in circumstances where a court finds itself unable to rule on an effective remedy in the absence of a party. Subscribing to the notion, as above expound that the Doctrine of Lis Pendens does not make a transaction pendent lite invalid, the court in the Anil Ranjan Ghosh Case ruled that a purchaser assignee of suit land being interested in the result of the suit can indeed be added as a party given his presence is necessary in the suit. Mr. Biswas has also drawn our attention to the judgment in Nathu Dhoju vs. Ramchand Balchand reported in AIR (33) 1946 Bombay 462 that addresses the risk that a transferee pendente lite may be exposed to in circumstances where a compromise is struck between the original litigants and there arises in the facts a fear that the compromise may not have been fairly and reasonably struck. In the Nathu Dhoju Case in fact it was held that if the final decision in any pending litigation is brought by any means less than fair then such decision shall not operate to affect the rights of the transferee pendente lite.
